# Introduction

Creativity is widely regarded as a fundamental human competency, yet how to
measure it remains a live and unresolved methodological problem across
psychology, education, and applied fields -- not a solved technical detail
[@long2022]. A taxonomy distinguishing the creative person, process, product,
and press (environment) has been proposed precisely because each facet
requires its own measurement logic and cannot be assessed by a single
all-purpose instrument [@batey2012; @barbot2019b]. As the concluding piece of
a recent special issue on creativity assessment argues, clarifying which
facet of creativity is being measured is a necessary precondition for judging
and improving any specific method [@barbot2019; @barbot2019b]. The present
paper is concerned with the *product* facet -- the creativity of a discrete,
observable outcome -- and with the subjective-judgment method that dominates
its assessment.

The consensual assessment technique (CAT) is the most widely used approach
to rating the creativity of products. Under CAT, judges with relevant
domain familiarity independently rate products' creativity without being
given a predefined rubric, on the logic that creativity is best captured as
a consensual, socially situated judgment rather than an objectively
specifiable property of the product itself [@amabile1982]. CAT has
accumulated a substantial track record of reasonable inter-rater agreement,
particularly once ratings are averaged across multiple judges, and treating
rater as a facet of measurement error within a generalizability-theory
framework has clarified how much of that error is attributable to raters
specifically [@long2015]. Textbook treatments now present CAT as a mature,
practically usable tool alongside divergent-thinking tests and self-report
measures [@kaufman2008].

Yet CAT's apparent maturity conceals a persistent, under-operationalized gap.
Cseh and Jeffries [-@cseh2019] offer a systematic critique of the technique,
arguing that CAT's validity depends on the correct use of a sufficient
number of judges with an appropriate level of expertise, and that both the
required number and the required expertise are properties of the specific
product and domain being rated -- they cannot be fixed once and for all
across applications. On this view, every new domain in which CAT is applied
owes the field its own empirical evidence on these design parameters. This
paper's central premise is that such evidence has not yet been supplied for
the domain of sport, and that this omission is representative of how CAT is
often applied to new domains more generally: with a design borrowed from
precedent rather than derived from domain-specific evidence.

## Sub-debate A: How many judges are enough?

A persistent rule of thumb in the CAT literature holds that "five to ten
judges" is generally adequate for most purposes [@kaufman2008].
<!-- CLAIM: the exact page/quote for this "5-10 judges" figure has not been
independently verified by the pipeline (see manuscript/04_outline.md, Evidence
gaps item 2); treat as a general heuristic, not a precisely sourced number,
until the author confirms the citation at the page level. -->
This heuristic is useful as a starting point but is not itself derived from
domain-specific empirical analysis. By contrast, generalizability-theory
approaches derive the number of judges (and items) required for a target
level of reliability directly from the data at hand, and have shown that
this number varies considerably by task type and rating design -- in one
divergent-thinking-rating context as few as three untrained raters combined
with four items sufficed for adequate dependability, but the estimate did
not generalize uniformly across designs [@hass2018]. The tension between a
generic heuristic and a domain-derived estimate is precisely the kind of gap
Cseh and Jeffries [-@cseh2019] identify, and it motivates this paper's first
research question.

## Sub-debate B: Does rater expertise matter, and how much?

A second, closely related debate concerns whether judges must be domain
experts. Amabile [-@amabile1982] argues that judges' level of experience need
not be uniform, and that CAT's reliability holds up even when the products
being rated are naturalistically produced and non-parallel -- that is, not
generated under identical, standardized experimental conditions. Direct
empirical support for this claim comes from studies showing that CAT
inter-rater reliability remained high when expert judges rated creative
writing produced under a variety of different assignments rather than a
single controlled prompt [@baer2004], and from design-engineering research
modeling how novices and experts differ in the knowledge they bring to
evaluating creative work [@christiaans2005]. At the same time, direct
comparisons of expert and non-expert raters using CAT show that non-experts
can be meaningfully discerning judges of creative products, complicating any
simple assumption that only experts should be recruited [@kaufman2008b].
Further evidence suggests that domain expertise does not straightforwardly
increase rater agreement: in a comparison of movie ratings, raters who had
simply seen more movies -- regardless of formal expert status -- correlated
more highly with professional critics than less-exposed raters did
[@plucker2009], suggesting that high exposure or experience can substitute,
at least partially, for formal expertise. This "heavy viewer" finding
directly motivates a design choice pursued below: recruiting football raters
who differ in exposure and background rather than assuming only coaches or
professionals can serve as valid judges. Other work argues that
domain-specific expertise nonetheless matters for some purposes
[@baer2015], and a further strand of research cautions that expertise itself
can introduce systematic biases -- a "dark side of expertise" in which
greater knowledge does not uniformly translate into better judgment
[@castel2007]. Rather than treating "expert" and "novice" as monolithic
categories, recent work has begun asking what individual-difference factors
predict discernment among novice raters specifically [@ceh2021]. This
sub-debate is presented here as genuinely open, not settled, and is the
subject of this paper's second research question.

## Sub-debate C: How should ratings from multiple, non-interchangeable judges be aggregated?

A third, more technical debate concerns aggregation. The conventional
practice of averaging ratings across judges implicitly treats judges as
exchangeable random effects -- interchangeable sources of measurement error
that cancel out on average. This assumption ignores the possibility that
judges differ systematically in severity or leniency, a concern that has
motivated two related but historically separate psychometric traditions.
Judge Response Theory (JRT) proposes modeling judgments with item-response-
theory-style models in which judges, like test items, have their own
parameters (e.g., severity, discrimination), yielding latent creativity
estimates that are corrected for these differences rather than averaged over
them [@myszkowski2019]. This proposal has since been operationalized in an
open-source R package that fits JRT models to CAT-style judgment data
[@myszkowski2021] and has been extended into a book-length treatment of item
response theory for creativity measurement more broadly [@myszkowski2024],
with a recent application decomposing novelty and appropriateness as
separate latent components within an item-response-tree framework
[@myszkowski2025] -- a decomposition directly relevant to the two-dimensional
novelty x appropriateness scale adopted below. Independently, the
Many-Facet Rasch Model (MFRM) tradition, developed originally for
rater-mediated performance assessment, models rater severity as one of
several crossed facets alongside examinee ability and item difficulty, and
provides established diagnostics for detecting systematic rater effects such
as leniency, central tendency, and halo [@eckes2015; @myford2003;
@myford2004]. MFRM has been applied directly to creativity ratings, showing
that individual raters can be diagnosed and examinees reliably
differentiated despite idiosyncratic rater behavior [@primi2019; @hung2012].
Despite their shared logic, JRT and MFRM emerged from separate literatures
and have not, to our knowledge, been directly compared against one another
or against naive averaging in a creativity-rating context at scale. This
paper's third research question addresses that gap.

## Construct validity: Is creativity discriminable from adjacent constructs?

A further concern, orthogonal to the number and expertise of judges, is
whether the construct being rated -- creativity -- is empirically separable
from adjacent constructs that judges might conflate with it, such as
aesthetic appeal or technical execution. Amabile [-@amabile1982] recommends
that when CAT is applied to a new domain, judges should also rate such
secondary dimensions so that the creativity rating's discriminant and
construct validity can be assessed directly rather than assumed. This
recommendation is adopted here, using the standard definitional consensus
that creativity reflects the joint presence of novelty (originality) and
appropriateness (functionality, or fit to the constraints and goals of the
situation) [@runco2012]. This paper's fourth research question asks whether
creativity, aesthetic appeal, and technical correctness form empirically
distinct factors when rated concurrently on the same set of products.

## A practical measurement concern: Rater fatigue

Beyond these conceptual debates, a comparatively neglected practical
question is how long raters can perform a CAT-style rating task before the
quality or consistency of their judgments declines. This is a design
question relevant to any large-scale CAT study, not a sport-specific one,
and has been investigated directly in at least one prior study examining
whether CAT ratings remain reliable across extended rating sessions
[@barth2020]. This paper's fifth research question adapts that logic to the
football domain.

## Narrowing to football: Why this domain, and why now

Creativity is considered one of the key competencies to be developed and
evaluated in football players, and assessing it in an ecologically valid,
naturalistic environment is an explicit priority for the field
[@safardilha2019]. Much of the existing sport-creativity literature has
studied the creative *process* -- for example, divergent-thinking ability and
its development in players -- while the creative *product*, the discrete
in-game action itself, has received comparatively little attention
[@memmert2011]. One prior study has evaluated the creativity of football
actions directly, using a 0-10 expert rating scale, and demonstrated face
validity by showing that rated creativity predicted the temporal proximity
of actions to goals [@kempe2018]; however, this study did not investigate how
many judges were needed, whether rater expertise mattered, or how ratings
from multiple judges should best be aggregated. Two further, smaller-scale
analogues exist: a two-expert-judge design rating in-game creativity on a
1-10 scale achieved very high inter-judge correlation [@oboeuf2020], and a
training-transfer study used expert on-field creativity ratings to compare
functional-skills training against divergent-thinking training
[@zahno2022]. Neither of these studies systematically varied the number or
expertise of judges, nor did either apply JRT or MFRM to model rater
severity. To our knowledge, no CAT-in-sport study to date has systematically
varied judge number or expertise, or modeled rater severity using modern
rater-effects models, in this domain.

## Aim and research questions

The aim of the present paper is to generate a large-scale, systematically
varied multi-rater creativity-rating dataset for a sports domain (football
actions) and to use it to provide the field with empirically grounded,
reproducible guidance on the psychometric design choices that Cseh and
Jeffries [-@cseh2019] argue cannot be resolved in general. Specifically, the
paper addresses the following research questions and, where the existing
literature already supports a directional prediction, states it as an
explicit hypothesis rather than leaving the question hypothesis-free by
omission:

- **RQ1 (judges).** How many raters are needed for stable, convergent
  creativity ratings of football actions?
  - **H1.** Inter-rater reliability (ICC) will increase with the number of
    judges averaged into the aggregate rating, with asymptotically
    diminishing returns, consistent with generalizability-theory/
    Spearman-Brown logic and with the empirical template set by Hass et al.
    [-@hass2018], who derived comparable judge/item-count curves in a
    different rating domain.
- **RQ2 (expertise).** Does rater expertise or exposure affect inter-rater
  agreement or rater severity? The Amabile-versus-Plucker/Kaufman tension
  developed in Sub-debate B above yields two competing, directional
  hypotheses rather than a single predicted winner; the RQ2 analyses test
  which position this dataset supports.
  - **H2a (Amabile-consistent).** Rater expertise level will not
    systematically affect agreement or severity.
  - **H2b (Plucker/Kaufman-consistent).** Non-expert but high-exposure
    raters will show agreement or severity comparable to, or exceeding,
    that of formally credentialed experts.
- **RQ3 (aggregation/psychometrics).** Do Judge Response Theory and/or
  Many-Facet Rasch Model rater-severity models improve on simple mean
  aggregation, and what do they reveal about individual raters? This
  question is stated as open/exploratory, with no directional hypothesis:
  JRT, MFRM, and naive averaging have not previously been compared
  head-to-head at this scale in a creativity-rating context, so there is no
  established prior result from which to derive a directional prediction.
- **RQ4 (construct validity).** What is the factor structure relating
  creativity, aesthetic appeal, and technical-correctness ratings? This
  question is likewise stated as open/exploratory: the factor structure
  among these three constructs is not yet established in this domain.
- **RQ5 (reliability over time).** How long can raters perform the rating
  task reliably before agreement or rating quality declines? This question
  is stated as open/exploratory: no prior football-specific, or more
  broadly sport-specific, fatigue/session-length data exist to ground a
  directional prediction.

This paper addresses these five measurement questions only. Correlating
rated creativity with performance outcomes (e.g., the value of possessions
added metric, VAEP, or player market value) and developing automated or
machine-learning-based creativity scoring are both explicitly deferred to
two companion papers; the present paper is intended to establish the
measurement foundation on which those applications will depend. Because RQ2
speaks directly to the practical question of who should be recruited as a
rater in future football-creativity studies -- coaches and other domain
experts, or high-exposure non-expert viewers -- resolving it is intended as
one of this paper's principal applied contributions to sport science, a
point returned to in the Discussion and Conclusion.

# Methods

This section describes a fully specified, reproducible proposed design.
Because data collection has not yet occurred, all procedures are described
in the future tense; nothing reported below has yet been executed.

## Design overview

This will be a cross-sectional, multi-rater creativity-rating study of
discrete football actions. The design combines a benchmark structure, in
which a fixed subset of actions is rated by every judge in the rater panel,
with a larger pairwise/rotating structure, in which a much larger set of
actions is rated by only two to three judges each. The benchmark subset
will enable full-overlap reliability analyses (RQ1-RQ3) at every candidate
judge count, while the pairwise subset will allow the dataset to scale
beyond what a fully crossed design could support within the available rater
capacity. The benchmark panel will comprise a fixed set of **10 raters**,
each of whom rates the full benchmark subset; this yields ICC/agreement
trajectories at every candidate judge count from 1 through 10 (see
"Judges/raters" and Analysis Plan (a) below). A panel of this size is large
enough that the study can directly test the generic "five to ten judges"
heuristic [@kaufman2008] against its own benchmark data, rather than merely
citing the heuristic secondhand -- a genuine strength of this design, since
the resulting ICC-by-judge-count curve spans exactly the range the
heuristic claims is sufficient.

## Stimuli: Sample of football actions

Video and event data will be sourced preferentially from StatsBomb (pending
confirmation of video access) or, as a fallback, from WyScout 17/18. Matches
will be sampled across multiple competitions, including men's and women's
FIFA tournaments, the Africa Cup of Nations, UEFA tournaments, and the Copa
America, in order to capture a broad range of playing contexts and player
populations.

The target sample is a purposive selection of approximately **1,000 to
2,000 football actions**, pre-selected as plausible creative-moment
candidates rather than drawn through exhaustive or random sampling of every
action in every match. Candidate actions might be identified via event-data
heuristics (e.g., flags for unusual pass trajectories, dribbles, or shot
techniques) or through expert pre-screening designed to surface actions
likely to vary meaningfully in creativity.
<!-- CLAIM: the exact operational criteria for "plausible creative-moment
candidate" pre-selection (rule-based heuristics vs. expert pre-screening,
and how the two might be combined) still need to be fully specified before
data collection begins; this is an explicit open item for the author to
resolve, not a settled design detail. -->

### Sample-size justification

The ~1,000-2,000-action target is, at present, a plausibility-based design
choice rather than the product of a formal a priori sample-size or power
calculation, and no such calculation has yet been performed. A more
rigorous alternative, should the author wish to pursue it before data
collection begins, would be precision-based planning conducted within a
generalizability-theory (G-theory) framework: for each candidate number of
judges under consideration for the benchmark subset, the minimum benchmark
size required to achieve a target confidence-interval width for the
resulting intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) could be estimated in
advance, following the logic used by Hass et al. [-@hass2018] to empirically
derive the number of raters and items needed for acceptable reliability of
divergent-thinking ratings. This is presented here as a decision point for
the author: either (a) proceed with the ~1,000-2,000-action purposive target
as currently planned, treating it as a plausible and logistically feasible
starting point, or (b) conduct a formal precision- or power-based
calculation first and adjust the target accordingly. As of this writing,
option (a) is the operative plan, and this should be understood as a
provisional rather than a finalized decision.

## Judges/raters

Raters will be recruited to span an expertise gradient, including both
domain experts (e.g., coaches or other football professionals) and
non-expert but high-exposure viewers (e.g., committed spectators without
formal coaching or playing credentials). This recruitment plan directly
operationalizes the Amabile-versus-Plucker/Kaufman expertise debate outlined
in the Introduction [@amabile1982; @kaufman2008; @kaufman2008b;
@plucker2009; @baer2015; @castel2007; @ceh2021]: rather than assuming a
single "correct" level of expertise, the design will allow expertise and
exposure effects on agreement and rater severity to be estimated directly
from the data.

The rater panel will be organized into two overlapping subsets. A fixed
benchmark panel of **10 raters** will rate every action in the benchmark
subset, enabling full pairwise ICC and agreement comparisons at every
candidate judge count from a single judge up to the full panel of 10 (see
Analysis Plan (a); the rationale for this panel size is given in Design
overview above). A larger pairwise/rotating subset of actions will be rated
by only two to three judges per action, drawn from the benchmark panel
and/or a separate pool of additional pairwise-only raters; the exact size of
this additional pool is not yet fixed and will depend on recruitment
logistics -- this is stated explicitly here as an open item, not invented.
The total rater pool for the study is therefore the 10-rater benchmark panel
plus this additional, as-yet-unsized pairwise-only pool.

Raters assigned to the pairwise subset will be allocated to actions via
random assignment constrained to preserve a connected rater-by-action
network -- that is, assignment will not be fully unconstrained, but
constrained so that the resulting rater-by-action bipartite graph remains
connected, a standard requirement for JRT/MFRM parameter identifiability.
This constraint partially de-risks, but does not eliminate, the
rater-by-action sparsity concern discussed in Limitations below:
connectivity is guaranteed by design, but the realized degree of overlap
remains unknown until data collection occurs.

## Rating instrument

Actions will be rated on a 7-point unipolar novelty x appropriateness scale,
with behaviorally anchored verbal descriptions at each scale point, following
psychometric guidance on selecting an appropriate number of response
categories. In addition to the primary creativity rating, judges will also
rate two secondary dimensions -- aesthetic appeal and technical correctness
-- for construct-validity purposes, following Amabile's [-@amabile1982]
recommendation that secondary constructs be rated alongside creativity
whenever CAT is applied to a new domain, and following the standard
definitional consensus that creativity itself reflects the joint presence of
novelty and appropriateness [@runco2012]. Judges will undergo a
frame-of-reference (FOR) training procedure prior to rating, intended to
calibrate their use of the scale's anchor points before live ratings begin:
raters will review a set of worked/anchor examples at each of the scale's
seven points, followed by a short calibration rating set with feedback,
before proceeding to live rating. This training session is expected to take
approximately 30-45 minutes, and raters will be required to reach an
agreement of at least .70 (e.g., intraclass correlation or an equivalent
percentage-agreement-within-one-scale-point criterion, with the exact index
to be finalized alongside the main analysis pipeline) with criterion or
consensus ratings on the calibration set before being approved to proceed to
live rating; raters who do not meet this threshold will repeat calibration
with an additional set of worked examples. This calibration protocol is a
plausible, generic design choice consistent with standard FOR-training
practice, and has not itself been piloted. Raters will view full match
footage and context, including player and team identity, rather than
blinded or anonymized clips, prioritizing ecological validity -- creativity
judgments grounded in naturalistic match footage rather than standardized,
blinded stimuli -- over experimental blinding (see Limitations for the
corresponding halo-effect risk). An explicit conversion bridge will be
specified between this 7-point scale and the 0-10 scale used by Kempe and
Memmert [-@kempe2018], to allow cross-study comparability with that
benchmark study.

## Procedure

Ratings will be collected via a dedicated rating platform presenting actions
in randomized order and exporting structured rating data for analysis; the
specific platform has not yet been selected and is flagged here, like the
additional pairwise-rater-pool size above and the pre-selection criteria in
"Stimuli," as an open item to be finalized by the author before data
collection. A pilot phase will precede full data collection, in which
per-session rating capacity will be established by monitoring agreement and
rating consistency as a function of position within the rating session;
this pilot directly informs RQ5 and follows the design logic of a prior
study examining CAT reliability over extended sessions [@barth2020].

## Analysis plan

Six analyses are planned. Five map directly onto the five research
questions above; the sixth, (b), is an auxiliary/supporting analysis for
RQ2 rather than an independent research question of its own (see (b)
below). All six analyses (a)-(f) commit, as a matter of design, to
reporting confidence intervals and effect sizes alongside, or instead of,
significance tests.

**(a) Judge-count convergence (RQ1).** Intraclass correlation coefficients
(e.g., ICC(2,k) or ICC(3,k), as appropriate to the design) will be computed
on the benchmark subset and examined as a function of the number of raters
averaged into the aggregate rating (k = 1 through the full 10-rater panel),
with a possible Spearman-Brown-type reliability projection to candidate
judge counts beyond those directly observed. A target reliability of
ICC(2,k) >= .80 is pre-specified as the criterion for declaring ratings
"stable/convergent" for the purposes of RQ1, with ICC(2,k) >= .70 noted as
a minimum acceptable floor, following standard convention in the
reliability/psychometrics literature; the number of judges "needed" will be
read off the ICC-by-judge-count curve against this pre-specified threshold,
not chosen post hoc. This analysis is motivated by Cseh and Jeffries'
[-@cseh2019] critique and follows the empirical, G-theory-informed template
set out by Hass et al. [-@hass2018], providing a direct, domain-specific
counterpart to the generic "five to ten judges" heuristic [@kaufman2008].

**(b) Variance-source mixed model (auxiliary analysis for RQ2).** A
mixed-effects model of the form
`rating ~ covariates + (1|rater) + (1|player) + (1|match)` will be fit to
partition variability in ratings across rater, player, and match sources
and to estimate the effect of any relevant covariates, including rater
expertise. This model is an auxiliary, supporting analysis for RQ2 rather
than an independent sixth research question: it decomposes rating variance
into rater/player/match sources and allows expertise to be entered as a
covariate or moderator, directly informing the H2a/H2b comparison described
in the Introduction.

**(c) Rater-severity diagnostics via JRT and MFRM (RQ3).** Rater severity
and leniency will be modeled using Judge Response Theory and/or the
Many-Facet Rasch Model, and the resulting rater-corrected estimates will be
compared against simple mean aggregation [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021;
@myszkowski2024; @myszkowski2025; @eckes2015; @myford2003; @myford2004;
@primi2019; @hung2012].

**(d) Expertise-group comparison (RQ2).** Agreement statistics (ICC) and/or
rater-severity parameters from the JRT/MFRM models will be compared across
expertise groups; expertise will also be entered as a covariate or moderator
in the mixed model described above.

**(e) Factor analysis (RQ4).** An exploratory and/or confirmatory factor
analysis will be conducted across the creativity, aesthetic-appeal, and
technical-correctness ratings to evaluate their dimensional structure
[@amabile1982].

**(f) Fatigue/session-duration reliability (RQ5).** Agreement and rating
consistency will be examined as a function of session position or
time-on-task, using the pilot data described above, following the design
logic of Barth and Stadtmann [-@barth2020].

### Software and estimation

The full analysis pipeline will be implemented within a single open-source,
reproducible R environment. JRT models will be fit using the `jrt` R package
[@myszkowski2021]. MFRM models will be fit using an R-based implementation:
the Test Analysis Modules package (TAM) for a standard many-facet Rasch
model, or, as an alternative, a Bayesian many-facet Rasch model fit via
`brms`, with rater, player/examinee, and item specified as crossed random
facets [@eckes2015; @myford2003; @myford2004]. Commercial Facets software
will not be used. This keeps JRT estimation, MFRM estimation, the mixed
models, and the factor analysis all reproducible from a single R codebase.

## Ethics statement

Ethics approval for this project was obtained from the Ethics Committee of
the German Sport University Cologne (approval no. 248/2025). This study was
not preregistered.

# Results

This section anticipates the results bearing on the five research questions
set out above -- the number of judges needed for convergent ratings, the
effect of rater expertise, whether JRT and MFRM rater-severity models
improve on naive averaging, the factor structure separating creativity from
adjacent constructs, and the reliability of ratings over session duration.
No data have yet been collected, and no numerical results are reported in
this section. What follows is a structural description of the results that
will be reported once data collection and analysis are complete, organized
in the same order as the research questions above. Each planned result is
linked to the corresponding placeholder object.

## Sample description

Once data collection is complete, @tbl-sample-description will report the
achieved number of distinct football actions rated, the number of matches
and competitions sampled, the number of judges recruited (against the
10-rater benchmark-panel target plus the additional pairwise-only rater
pool, whose size is still to be finalized), and the number of ratings
obtained per action in both the benchmark and pairwise subsets, set against
the ~1,000-2,000-action purposive target specified in Methods.

## RQ1: Judge-count convergence

@fig-icc-by-judge-count will show inter-rater reliability (ICC) as a
function of the number of judges included in the aggregate rating (k = 1
through 10), computed on the 10-rater benchmark subset rated by all judges.
@tbl-agreement-by-judge-count will tabulate the corresponding agreement and
reliability statistics, along with category-usage checks, across a set of
candidate judge counts (2, 3, 5, and 10 judges, all achievable from the
10-rater benchmark panel). Both will be read against the pre-specified
ICC(2,k) >= .80 target and .70 minimum floor stated in Methods, Analysis
Plan (a), to identify the number of judges needed for stable, convergent
ratings. Together these will address RQ1 and H1, and provide the empirical
counterpart to the general "five to ten judges" heuristic discussed in the
Introduction -- a comparison the 10-rater benchmark-panel design was built
to support directly.

## RQ2: Expertise effects

@fig-expertise-agreement will compare rater agreement and validity metrics
across expertise groups (e.g., domain experts vs. non-expert, high-exposure
raters), framed against the competing H2a/H2b hypotheses stated in the
Introduction, and @tbl-expertise-effects will report mixed-model estimates
of rater expertise as a predictor of rating level and/or variance, with
rater, player, and match modeled as random effects, per the
variance-source model specified in Methods (analysis (b) above, an
auxiliary analysis supporting RQ2). Whether the general
variance-decomposition mixed model (Methods, analysis (b)) is reported as

# Discussion

## Contribution and place in the literature

This paper is intended as a direct empirical response to Cseh and Jeffries'
[-@cseh2019] call for domain-specific evidence on CAT's design parameters,
and as an applied test, at scale, of the rater-effects modeling program
initiated by Myszkowski and Storme [-@myszkowski2019]. Whatever the eventual
results, generating a large-scale, systematically varied multi-rater
creativity-rating dataset for football actions is itself a contribution:
prior sport-creativity research has never varied judge number or expertise
systematically, nor compared rater-effects models against naive averaging in
this domain.

**[TBC -- author to confirm once data are available]** The judge-count
finding (RQ1) will bear on what number of judges should be recommended for
football, and by extension similarly naturalistic, product-based creativity
studies, read against the pre-specified ICC(2,k) >= .80 target (.70 minimum
floor; Methods, Analysis Plan (a)). This eventual recommendation should be
explicitly compared against the generic "five to ten judges" heuristic
[@kaufman2008] (noting that the precise page-level source of this figure
remains unverified) and against the generalizability-theory-derived numbers
found in other rating domains [@hass2018] -- a comparison the 10-rater
benchmark-panel design was built to support directly. Whether the
football-specific number converges with, falls below, or exceeds these
comparators is not yet known.

**[TBC -- author to confirm once data are available]** The expertise finding
(RQ2) will indicate whether football creativity rating resolves toward
hypothesis H2a, Amabile's [-@amabile1982] position that expertise need not
be uniform across judges, or toward hypothesis H2b, the position that
domain expertise does not straightforwardly improve agreement
[@plucker2009; @kaufman2008b]. The practical question of who should be
recruited as a rater in future football-creativity studies -- coaches and
other domain experts, or high-exposure non-expert viewers -- depends
directly on this result.

**[TBC -- author to confirm once data are available]** The rater-severity
finding (RQ3) will speak to whether JRT and/or MFRM modeling is worth the
added analytic complexity relative to naive averaging for this kind of
naturalistic, non-parallel rating data. This positions the present study as
an applied test of the JRT research program [@myszkowski2021;
@myszkowski2024; @myszkowski2025] and of MFRM as an established alternative
[@primi2019; @hung2012; @eckes2015], with both estimated throughout in R
(`jrt`; TAM or `brms`) for full reproducibility.

**[TBC -- author to confirm once data are available]** The factor-structure
finding (RQ4) will indicate whether creativity is empirically discriminable
from aesthetic appeal and technical correctness in this domain, connecting
back to the taxonomy/facet-clarity argument that different facets of
creativity require distinct measurement treatment [@barbot2019b] and to
Amabile's [-@amabile1982] construct-validity rationale for rating secondary
dimensions alongside creativity.

**[TBC -- author to confirm once data are available]** The fatigue/
session-length finding (RQ5) will provide practical guidance for designing
CAT rating protocols generally, not only in sport, extending the precedent
set by Barth and Stadtmann [-@barth2020].

## Generalizability

Taken together, the eventual findings are intended to inform CAT practice
broadly, directly answering Cseh and Jeffries' [-@cseh2019] call for
domain-specific empirical evidence on judge number, expertise, and
aggregation method. At the same time, a single applied domain -- football --
cannot by itself resolve a domain-general question; the extent to which
these findings transfer to other creative-product domains remains an open
question for future replication.

## Limitations

- This study addresses a single applied domain (football); generalization
  of any findings to other creative-product domains is an open question.
  Football's naturalistic, non-parallel-stimulus character (Methods, "Design
  overview") makes it a demanding test case, however, so findings that hold
  here are plausible candidates for transfer to other applied domains.
- Rater recruitment is convenience- and plan-dependent, and the exact
  operationalization of "expertise" (e.g., which credentials or exposure
  thresholds distinguish expert from non-expert raters) still needs to be
  finalized before data collection. Recruiting explicitly along an expertise
  gradient (Methods, "Judges/raters") is nonetheless the design feature that
  makes RQ2 testable at all, rather than an incidental shortcoming.
- The "five to ten judges" heuristic's exact source page has not been
  independently verified; it should not be cited as a precisely sourced
  figure until confirmed.
- The identifiability of the MFRM/JRT models depends on the realized
  sparsity of the rater-by-action rating matrix, which is not yet known and
  cannot be guaranteed in advance of data collection; the constrained
  random-assignment rule described in Methods ("Judges/raters") guarantees
  a connected rater-by-action network by design, which partially de-risks
  but does not eliminate this concern -- the realized degree of overlap
  remains unknown until data collection occurs.
- Raters will view full match footage and context, including player and
  team identity, rather than blinded or anonymized clips (Methods, "Rating
  instrument"), prioritizing ecological validity over blinding; this
  introduces a plausible halo-effect risk, in which recognizable players or
  teams could influence creativity judgments independently of the action
  itself. The Many-Facet Rasch Model (Sub-debate C; Analysis Plan (c)) is
  explicitly intended to help diagnose such rater idiosyncrasies, including
  halo effects, but cannot fully substitute for blinding.
- Rater fatigue and motivation effects in a large-scale, potentially
  online/remote rating task are a genuine risk; no dedicated Results
  artifact is currently planned for the fatigue/session-length finding
  (RQ5), and a dedicated fatigue-analysis output still needs to be finalized
  in a future results-embedder pass once pilot data exist. The planned pilot
  phase (Methods, "Procedure") is designed explicitly to surface this risk
  before full-scale data collection begins.
- The purposive (non-random) sampling of "plausible creative-moment"
  actions means that prevalence or base-rate claims about creativity in
  football cannot be supported by this sample; only relative, psychometric
  comparisons (judge-count, expertise, aggregation method) are licensed by
  this design.
- No formal a priori sample-size or power calculation was performed for the
  ~1,000-2,000-action target; it reflects a plausibility-based design
  decision rather than a precision-targeted calculation (see Methods).
  Methods already sets out how such a calculation could be performed
  ("Sample-size justification"), leaving a clear path to strengthen this
  before data collection if the author chooses.
- This study was not preregistered.

# Conclusion

This paper proposes an empirically grounded, reproducible methodological
template for consensual-assessment-technique-based creative-product rating
in sport, directly addressing a domain-specificity gap that the broader
creativity-assessment literature has repeatedly flagged but rarely
operationalized [@cseh2019].

**[TBC -- author to confirm once data are available]** Once the planned
analyses are complete, this paper will offer practical recommendations for
future sport-creativity CAT studies concerning the number of judges to
recruit, the expertise mix of the rater panel, and whether rater-effects
modeling (JRT/MFRM) is worth adopting over simple averaging. Resolving the
expertise question (RQ2) in particular is intended as one of the paper's
principal applied contributions to sport science, since it bears directly
on who should be recruited as a rater in future studies. These
recommendations are contingent on the Results and Discussion above and are
not stated as specific numbers here.

This paper is the first of a planned three-paper sequence. A companion
application paper will examine the relationship between rated creativity
and performance outcomes such as the value of possessions added (VAEP) and
player market value; a further companion paper will explore automated,
machine-learning-based creativity scoring, using the human ratings generated
here as ground truth -- following a precedent, in the same target journal,
for validating automated scoring against consensual-assessment-technique
ratings of creative products [@distefano2024]. Both are named here only as
future work and are not elaborated further. Getting the human measurement
foundation right is treated here as a precondition for both of these
follow-on efforts.
